title: Knowing your price
hook: Agrippinus kept his character though it cost him; each person knows their own price (Discourses 1.2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the tyrant's room, and the will no one can chain. Your line was what is still yours. What did you find was still yours inside a constraint? Day three hundred ninety-one.

Agrippinus is being tried before the Senate in Rome. A messenger runs to tell him. Agrippinus says: good luck to it. But it's the hour for exercise and a cold bath. Let's go. Later the messenger comes back. You've been condemned. To exile, or to death? Exile. And my property? Not taken. Then let's go out to Aricia and have lunch. Epictetus tells that one in the first discourse. In the second, he tells another story about him, about a question Agrippinus refused even to think about. Today: knowing your price.
screen: `AGRIPPINUS, ON TRIAL.` → `EXILE? THEN LET'S HAVE LUNCH.` → `KNOWING YOUR PRICE.`

segments.voice: First, the question. The second discourse is titled, roughly, how to keep your own character in everything. The Greek word for character there is prosōpon, the mask and role we met in the handbook. Second, the chamber pot. Epictetus imagines someone asking whether to hold the chamber pot for another man. If he refuses, he'll be beaten and go without food. For a different person, it would be unbearable not only to hold it, but even to let someone else hold it for him. If you ask me, Epictetus says, I'll tell you food is worth more than hunger and a beating is worse than none, so if that's how you measure, go and hold it. But it's beneath me? That, he says, is something you bring to the question, not me. You know yourself, what you're worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself. People sell themselves at different prices. Third, Agrippinus. A man named Florus was weighing whether to take part in one of Nero's spectacles, appearing on stage to please the emperor. He asked Agrippinus. Agrippinus said: go. Then why won't you? Because, said Agrippinus, I don't even consider the question. Fourth, the point of that answer. Once you start weighing such things, Epictetus says, setting the value of outside things against each other, you're close to those who've forgotten their own character. Agrippinus didn't win the argument about Nero's stage. He never let it become an argument. Knowing your price isn't about being proud. It's knowing, before the offer arrives, the few things that simply aren't for sale.
screen: `KEEP YOUR CHARACTER IN EVERYTHING.` · `YOU KNOW AT WHAT PRICE YOU SELL YOURSELF.` · `I DON'T EVEN CONSIDER THE QUESTION.` · `SOME THINGS AREN'T FOR SALE.` · then, large: `I KNOW MY PRICE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself, quietly: what wouldn't I do, even if it paid well, even if everyone else was doing it? Not in theory. In your actual week. Laughing at a cruel joke to fit in. Shading the truth for a sale. Flattering someone to get ahead. Find one. Now picture the moment it's offered, and picture yourself not even weighing it. Just a plain no. The bell holds the time.
Agrippinus. The man who wouldn't even consider some questions; you know at what price you sell yourself. Today's word.
Your line: I know my price. Refuse one thing beneath you today, without weighing it, the way Agrippinus refused Nero's stage. Day three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes decide in advance on a few things they will not do for any reward, so that when the offer comes they don't have to deliberate.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.1.28–32 (Agrippinus' trial and lunch at Aricia)

notes: Discourses 1.1.28–32 paraphrased: Agrippinus told he is being tried in the Senate; goes to exercise and bathe; condemned to exile; property not confiscated; 'let us go to Aricia and dine'. Confirm section numbers.

Discourses 1.2 paraphrased: title on preserving one's character (prosōpon) in everything; the chamber-pot example; 'you know how much you are worth to yourself and at what price you sell yourself; men sell themselves at different prices'; Florus considering going down to Nero's spectacles; Agrippinus: 'go down'; 'I do not even consider the question'; whoever stoops to such consideration is near to forgetting his character. Confirm.
1.2 also contains a passage about suicide by hanging as an example of the 'reasonable'; deliberately omitted.
Helvidius Priscus and the purple stripe (also in 1.2) are left for tomorrow.

The chamber-pot holder is glossed as 'an enslaved man asking whether to hold the chamber pot for his master'; the Greek speaks of holding it for another, with beating and loss of food as the stakes, which implies servitude but does not name it. Confirm the gloss is fair.
The hook places Agrippinus' trial 'under Nero'; Paconius Agrippinus was exiled in 66/67 (Tacitus, Annals 16.28-33). Epictetus' account does not name the emperor in 1.1. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'under Nero' from the trial (1.1 does not name the emperor) and 'Epictetus loved this man' (unsourced); chamber-pot passage corrected: the second man finds it intolerable even to have another hold it for him (not 'to watch someone else do it'), and the asker is no longer labeled enslaved, since the text does not say so.
